steps.prompt: Your friend says, “Our town needs a skate park.” You ask, “Why should I believe you?” What could they say to convince you?

cards.title: Evidence: prove it
cards.body: Evidence supports your topic sentence. It can be a fact or number (“Teens need 8–10 hours of sleep.”), an example (“For example, my brother…”), a quote from a text, or what an expert says (“According to…”).

cards.title: Explanation: so what?
cards.body: Evidence never speaks for itself. After each piece, explain what it shows and how it supports your main idea. Start with “This shows that…”, “This means…” or “As a result, …”.

cards.title: Evidence + explanation
cards.text:
Topic: Our town needs a skate park.
Evidence: Last year, police gave 40 warnings to skaters in the mall car park.
Explanation: This shows that teens have nowhere safe to skate, so they use places that are dangerous.
cards.note: The explanation links the evidence back to the topic sentence.

cards.title: Don’t drop the evidence and run
cards.telling: Teens need 8–10 hours of sleep. School starts at 7:30.
cards.showing: Teens need 8–10 hours of sleep. This means a 7:30 start forces many of them to come to class tired.

prompts: Which kind of evidence (fact, example, quote, expert) do you find easiest to use? Which is most convincing?
Why does evidence need an explanation after it?
